name: Funj Sultanate of Sennar
summary: A Muslim sultanate on the Blue and White Nile that replaced the Christian kingdom of Alwa; it lasted until Egypt under Muhammad Ali conquered it in 1821.

location.value: Sennar, on the Blue Nile. The article never defines the Gezira’s boundaries.

terrain.value: A flat clay plain between the Blue and White Nile, with seasonal rivers and some hills.

climate.value: Hot and dry for most of the year, with summer rains from June to September.

resources.value: Grain (sorghum), cotton, gold from the south, ivory and livestock.

disasters.value: Famines after poor rains and occasional epidemics.

population.value: The article gives no population estimate; military estimates: about 5,000 horsemen at the peak and about 14,000 infantry in 1772.

urbanisation.value: Mostly villages; a royal capital and market towns.

disease.value: Malaria and other tropical diseases; smallpox outbreaks.

migration.value: Arab nomadic groups moved into the region, mixing with the Funj and local peoples.

economicBase.value: Mostly farming, on land that technically belonged to the sultan. Gold was the main currency. Lords paid tribute in cloth, gold, ivory and horses. The state tried to monopolise the slave trade to Egypt (caravans of up to 1,000 slaves a year) and charged customs on caravan routes.

tradeRoutes.value: Caravans carried gold, slaves and ivory north to Egypt and east to the Red Sea ports.

wealth.value: All caravans were controlled by the monarch, and the sultanate monopolised the slave trade to Egypt.

moneyAndTax.value: Tribute, market taxes and trade goods; cowrie shells in many markets.

inequality.value: Rulers and nobles above free farmers; enslaved people at the bottom.

governmentType.value: A sultanate; from 1762 the Hamaj regency made the Funj monarchs puppets.

keyRulers.value: Amara Dunqas (first sultan, 1503–1533/4), Badi II (1644/5–81), Badi IV (1724–62), and Badi VII, the last sultan, who submitted in 1821.

succession.value: The sultan came from the royal family, but after 1762 the Hamaj regents held real power.

institutions.value: Sufi scholars, local chiefs and the royal court at Sennar ran justice and religion.

stability.value: The Hamaj regents took power in 1762 and the sultans became figureheads.

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry between the Funj royal family and the Hamaj regents.

armyAndTech.value: Cavalry and slave soldiers, with some firearms in the late period.

majorWars.value: Battle of Hannik (1585), where the Funj crushed the Ottomans.

territoryChange.value: Expanded west toward Kordofan in the 1600s and shrank by the late 1700s.

alliancesRivals.value: Ethiopia to the east, the Ottomans in Egypt to the north, and Darfur to the west.

scienceEducation.value: Oral learning; Qur’anic schools where Islam spread.

openness.value: Open to trade and Muslim scholars, but wary of rival states.

communicationTransport.value: Footpaths, the Nile and caravan routes carried people and messages.

religion.value: Islam. Conversion was at first only nominal; the page calls it an African empire with a Muslim façade until the 18th century. Rulers sponsored Muslim holy men and used Arabic for administration and trade.

languageWriting.value: Arabic was used for religion and records, with local languages spoken.

artsArchitecture.value: The old mosque of Sennar, mud-brick buildings and tombs of holy men.

socialStructure.value: Funj nobles, Arab tribes, farmers and captives.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the sultan and to Islam bound the many groups.

dailyLife.value: Most families farmed sorghum and herded animals in villages along the rivers.

ideasReligions.value: The sultanate invited Sufi holy men to settle; the date when the Funj adopted Islam is not known.

colonisation.value: Conquered by Egypt (under Ottoman rule) in 1821.

riseSignals.value: Established in 1504 by Sultan Amara Dunqas, a convert to Islam; the capital was Sennar.

peakPeriod.value: The end of the 1600s. The page says Sennar was at its peak at the end of the 17th century.

declineSignals.value: Regent rule after 1762 and Egyptian conquest in 1821.

outcome.value: Conquered by Turco-Egyptian forces; Badi VII submitted on 14 June 1821.

overallCertainty.value: Known from oral traditions, travellers and colonial records; many dates are approximate.
